source_refs.note: Topic 19.10 (PDF 56); Figure 19.7 is redrawn. The racemic-mixture and chiral-catalyst sentence follows the learning outcome; the claim that thalidomide will never be marketed again is corrected. Exercises (PDF 56-58) are not included.

blocks.text: In making medicines, chirality is critical for safety and effectiveness. Living systems are built from chiral building blocks, and drug receptors act as highly specific chiral locks, so the two enantiomers of a chiral drug often have very different effects.

blocks.alt: Skeletal structure of thalidomide: a benzene ring fused to a five-membered ring with two C=O groups and an N, joined through that N to a six-membered ring containing two C=O groups and an N-H. The carbon joined to the first N carries an H and is circled and starred as the chiral carbon.
blocks.caption: Thalidomide and its chiral carbon (original structure after Figure 19.7).
blocks.long_description: Thalidomide has one chiral carbon, the ring carbon bonded to nitrogen, so it exists as two enantiomers. It was sold as the racemic mixture. In the body each enantiomer is quickly converted into the other, so even a pure single isomer becomes racemic soon after it is taken.

blocks.text: Thalidomide was first sold as a racemic mixture and seemed a very successful, non-toxic sedative (tranquilliser) with no known side effects. In the early 1960s, however, it was found that women given it for nausea ('morning sickness') in early pregnancy had babies with severe deformities, and the drug was withdrawn at once. Research showed that the (+) isomer was an effective and safe tranquilliser while the (-) isomer harmed the fetus. At first the problem was blamed on contamination by the (-) isomer in some batches, but later work showed that the pure (+) isomer racemises rapidly in the bloodstream: within 10 minutes the racemisation is more than 50% complete.
